articles.title: 10 Questions to Ask Before Moving in Together
articles.content_markdown: Before you share an address, are you also ready to share the unglamorous parts of daily life, like money, chores, privacy, and what happens when one of you is stressed or annoyed? Moving in together changes more than your zip code. It turns two separate routines into one shared system, and that system works best when both people have already talked through the details instead of hoping they'll “figure it out later.” The smartest **questions to ask before moving in together** aren't about whether you love each other enough. They're about how you'll handle the rent, the dishes, the quiet hours, the family drop-ins, and the moments when you need space but still want to feel connected. A simple way to do this is to answer separately first, compare notes, name the practical details, agree on a first version, and set a date to revisit it. Differences don't have to be dealbreakers. They can be the starting point for real agreements. ## Table of Contents - [1. How do we handle finances and household expenses?](#1-how-do-we-handle-finances-and-household-expenses) - [Use language that makes money less loaded](#use-language-that-makes-money-less-loaded) - [2. What are our expectations around household chores and cleaning?](#2-what-are-our-expectations-around-household-chores-and-cleaning) - [3. How do we balance alone time and together time?](#3-how-do-we-balance-alone-time-and-together-time) - [4. What are our boundaries around family involvement?](#4-what-are-our-boundaries-around-family-involvement) - [5. How do we handle conflict and disagreements?](#5-how-do-we-handle-conflict-and-disagreements) - [6. What does intimacy and physical affection look like for each of us?](#6-what-does-intimacy-and-physical-affection-look-like-for-each-of-us) - [7. How do we handle stress, work, and mental health?](#7-how-do-we-handle-stress-work-and-mental-health) - [8. What are our expectations around social media, privacy, and technology?](#8-what-are-our-expectations-around-social-media-privacy-and-technology) - [9. Do we want kids, and if so, what does parenting look like?](#9-do-we-want-kids-and-if-so-what-does-parenting-look-like) - [10. How do we envision our future together, and what are our non-negotiable values?](#10-how-do-we-envision-our-future-together-and-what-are-our-non-negotiable-values) - [Moving In Together: 10-Point Comparison](#moving-in-together-10-point-comparison) - [Turn the Answers Into a Shared Home Plan](#turn-the-answers-into-a-shared-home-plan) ## 1. How do we handle finances and household expenses? Money should be one of the first conversations, not the awkward one you have after the first rent payment bounces around emotionally for a week. A 2024 Ipsos survey found that **34% of partnered Americans identify money as a source of conflict**, and **79% believe finances should be discussed relatively early** rather than postponed until after cohabitation, with **31%** saying the right time is when the couple is planning to live together ([Ipsos](https://www.ipsos.com/en-us/money-fights-one-three-34-partnered-americans-identify-money-source-conflict-their-relationship)). That lines up with the practical reality that moving in together changes how trust works, especially if one person earns more, carries debt, or feels sensitive about spending. Start with the simplest version of the question, then get more specific. Who pays rent, utilities, groceries, and shared subscriptions? Will you split everything evenly, or proportionally by income? If one of you already has a lease or owns the place, what happens to the deposit, and what written record will you keep of each person's contribution? Financial advisors recommend documenting deposit splits in writing, and landlords often assume the deposit was provided equally by all people on the lease ([Merrill Edge](https://www.merrilledge.com/article/checklist-moving-in-together)). ### Use language that makes money less loaded Try, “I want us to feel fair, not fuzzy. What split would feel workable to you?” If one of you is embarrassed about debt, anxiety, or uneven earnings, focus on transparency rather than perfection. Research on couple money talk suggests that people handle it better when they use self-disclosure, task-sharing, and relationship-focused conversation, not just bill-splitting (Couples Institute summary). A few practical agreements help fast: - **Pick a system for shared costs.** A shared spreadsheet, a budgeting app, or a joint account for household bills can make the arrangement visible. - **Set a spending check-in point.** Even a simple “let's ask each other before spending over our agreed limit” rule can prevent resentment. - **Choose a monthly money date.** Put it on the calendar so budgeting doesn't depend on whoever remembers first. - **Name money triggers.** One person may hate surprise purchases, while the other feels controlled by too many rules. LoveCheck's **Couple Quiz** in Classic mode can make this conversation feel lighter if you want a low-pressure way to compare money values before you sign anything. ## 2. What are our expectations around household chores and cleaning? Shared space gets messy in a very ordinary way, which is exactly why people underestimate it. No one usually breaks up over a dirty spoon. The problem is the slow buildup of feeling like the only adult in the apartment. Academic research has linked premarital cohabitation with more negative communication and lower satisfaction later on, and that makes concrete household expectations worth naming early ([PMC study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5956859/)). Ask the question in plain language, not in a cute, vague way. “What does a clean home look like to you?” is far more useful than “Are you tidy?” One person may mean “no dishes in the sink,” while the other means “nothing on the floor, ever.” If you don't define “clean enough,” you can both be trying and still frustrate each other. Here's what helps in real homes: - **Assign based on preference, not gender.** If one person doesn't mind bathrooms and the other hates them, use that. - **Make chores visible.** A whiteboard, shared note, fridge chart, or app keeps tasks from becoming invisible labor. - **Build in rotation.** Some couples swap chores every quarter so no one gets stuck with the same annoying job forever. - **Talk about support, not just standards.** “What would make the kitchen feel okay to you?” lands better than “Why haven't you done the dishes?” If both of you work long hours, hiring a cleaner every two weeks can be a practical choice instead of a luxury conversation. If that's not in budget, a **cleaning Sunday** works well for a lot of couples because it turns house maintenance into a shared routine instead of a silent complaint. > **Practical rule:** If you can't explain the chore system to a friend in one minute, it's probably too vague for two people sharing a home. ## 3. How do we balance alone time and together time? Moving in together does not mean being in the same room every waking hour. Some couples get tense because they assume closeness always looks like constant togetherness, when a healthier rhythm is usually more flexible. There's also a practical side to this now, especially for couples who work from home, blend home and office space, or need more decompression after a busy day. The question to ask is simple: “What does alone time look like for you?” For some people, it means being in a different room with headphones on. For others, it means leaving the apartment entirely. That difference matters because one partner may be asking for solitude and the other may hear rejection. A few real-life versions of good balance: - **Tuesday and Thursday are friend nights.** Each person does their own thing without guilt. - **Coffee together in the morning.** It's a small ritual, but it can keep the day from feeling scattered. - **A no-pressure arrival ritual.** When both of you get home, put the phones down for 15 minutes before talking logistics. - **One person goes to the gym, the other reads at home.** Separate activities don't signal distance when the relationship feels secure. NPR's moving-in survey includes questions about bedtime, waking time, sleep preferences, and alone time, which is a good reminder that these small rhythms are not small at all ([NPR-related survey reference](https://dspace.cuni.cz/handle/20.500.11956/203418)). If one of you needs quiet to reset and the other wants to talk the second the front door opens, the solution isn't “compromise” in the abstract. It's timing. LoveCheck's **Mood of the Day** quest can make these check-ins easier by giving you a quick way to notice who's energized, who's drained, and who needs a little space before connection. ## 4. What are our boundaries around family involvement? Families don't disappear when two people move in together, they often become more visible. Suddenly there are questions about visits, keys, holiday expectations, and how much of your relationship belongs to your relatives. That's why this talk works best before anyone is upset, not after a parent drops by unannounced and everyone pretends it was fine. Frame the conversation around protection, not rejection. You're not saying, “We don't want your family around.” You're saying, “We want our home to feel calm and respectful.” That distinction helps a lot, especially when one partner is closer to family than the other or when there's a habit of oversharing private relationship details. Useful boundaries sound like this: - **“Visits need notice.”** For example, parents can come by monthly, but not unannounced. - **“No family has a key.”** If you do give one out, agree on exactly who, why, and what gets communicated first. - **“We handle our own families.”** If there's a conflict, each person talks to their own side. - **“We keep relationship drama private.”** That line can save a lot of awkward triangulation. A small script helps if family members push for more access than you want: “This works best for us.” It's calm, clear, and not a debate invitation. If one of you tends to override the other under family pressure, name that early and agree it won't happen. Boundaries only work when both people back them in the moment. ## 5. How do we handle conflict and disagreements? Every couple has conflict. The question is whether your home becomes a place where arguments spiral or a place where both of you know how to reset. Research on relationship outcomes suggests that timing and communication patterns matter, and couples who cohabit before engagement have shown less favorable outcomes than those who live together later in the commitment process ([IFStudies executive summary](https://ifstudies.org/reports/whats-the-plan-cohabitation/2023/executive-summary)). That doesn't mean conflict is doomed, it means the way you handle it deserves real attention. Ask this early: “When you're upset, do you want to talk immediately, or do you need time alone first?” One partner may need to cool down in silence. The other may need quick reassurance. Neither style is wrong. The problem starts when each person assumes their own style is the only reasonable one. A better conflict plan can sound like this: > **If we're both calm, we come back to the conversation. If either of us is flooded, we take space and set a time to return.** That one sentence prevents a lot of half-finished fights. You can also agree on a soft restart phrase, like “Can we try that again more gently?” It sounds simple, but it can interrupt a sharp tone before the whole conversation turns defensive. A few ground rules help: - **Use “I” statements.** “I felt unheard when...” lands better than “You always...” - **Don't fight when hungry, tired, or overloaded.** That's not weakness, it's timing. - **Write it down if talking gets too hot.** Some couples do better exchanging notes and then talking later. - **End with one concrete next step.** “Who's taking the groceries?” is often better than a dramatic emotional truce that solves nothing. If you want a practice space for kinder conversations, LoveCheck's Daily Love Quests can support lighter vulnerability, and [these couple therapy exercises at home](https://www.lovecheckapp.com/blog/couple-therapy-exercises-at-home) can help you build the habit of repairing instead of rehearsing the same argument. ## 6. What does intimacy and physical affection look like for each of us? Intimacy gets redefined once you share a home. Sometimes that means more affection because you're around each other more. Sometimes it means less spontaneity because daily logistics start crowding out desire. A useful conversation starts with touch, not just sex, because people often need different kinds of closeness to feel wanted. Try asking, “What kind of physical affection makes you feel loved?” That can open the door to real answers. One partner might love hand-holding, forehead kisses, or hugging in the kitchen. The other might feel closest through acts of service and only warm up to touch after stress has settled. Neither is a problem. It's just information. A few ways couples make this more workable: - **Talk about non-sexual touch first.** It's easier and usually less loaded. - **Schedule intimacy if spontaneity isn't happening.** Planned time can be respectful, not mechanical. - **Create a low-pressure opt-out signal.** A simple “not tonight” without shame keeps rejection from turning into a fight. - **Check in about stress and libido.** Desire changes with life, and that's normal. - **Talk about privacy.** Shared housing changes when and how you get personal space. A direct but gentle question helps: “Are we both happy with our physical connection right now? What would feel better?” If you want a more playful entry point, LoveCheck's **Couple Quiz** in Spicy mode can help you compare preferences without making the first conversation feel clinical. For a deeper prompt set, [questions to feel closer to your partner](https://www.lovecheckapp.com/blog/questions-to-feel-closer-to-your-partner) can help you move past surface-level answers. ## 7. How do we handle stress, work, and mental health? Stress does not stay at the office door, and it does not respect relationship timing either. One person may come home full of words and need to vent for 20 minutes. The other may need quiet first. If you don't talk about that difference, stress can get misread as coldness, criticism, or withdrawal. Ask, “When you're stressed, do you want to talk, be distracted, or be left alone?” That question gives your partner a choice instead of forcing them into your preferred style of support. A person who needs decompression might say, “I'm running on empty. Give me 30 minutes and then I'll be more present.” That's much kinder than disappearing without explanation. A few supportive habits go a long way: - **Use a low-energy signal.** “I need extra grace today” can prevent unnecessary tension. - **Create a check-in ritual.** A quick “1 to 10, how are you doing?” helps you notice patterns. - **Keep work stress out of every meal.** Phone-free dinner or bedtime protects the relationship from becoming a second workplace. - **Support professional help when needed.** If depression, anxiety, addiction, betrayal, or a mental-health crisis is in the picture, reach out to a licensed professional. > **Helpful truth:** You're not responsible for solving your partner's stress, but you are responsible for how you show up around it. LoveCheck's **Mood of the Day** can make these check-ins feel less forced. It gives you a simple way to notice emotional weather before a bad day turns into a bad week. ## 8. What are our expectations around social media, privacy, and technology? A lot of couples say they've talked about “privacy” when they've really only talked about passwords. Those are not the same thing. The core question is how public you want your relationship to be, and how protected each person wants their private life to remain. Start with something simple: “How do you feel about sharing couple stuff online?” Some people love anniversary posts and vacation photos. Others want their relationship to stay mostly offline. Neither preference is strange. Trouble starts when one person posts freely and the other feels exposed or controlled. The most useful boundaries are concrete: - **No posting arguments.** Relationship struggles stay private. - **Ask before tagging.** That gives both people agency over their image. - **Keep phones out of the bedroom.** Sleep and intimacy both benefit. - **Make dinner phone-free at least once a week.** Even one protected meal can change the tone of a week. - **Respect special privacy needs.** If someone has trauma from an ex sharing personal details, that matters. If one partner has a public-facing job, discuss what that means for photos, captions, and location sharing. Fame doesn't have to be the issue, visibility does. The same goes for couples who prefer to keep love offline. You don't need a public explanation for wanting privacy. LoveCheck's [privacy page](https://www.lovecheckapp.com/privacy) is a good reminder that privacy is part of trust, not an afterthought. Make the same standard true in your home. ## 9. Do we want kids, and if so, what does parenting look like? This is one of those **questions to ask before moving in together** that can feel too big for a rental conversation, but it isn't. If one person wants children and the other doesn't, or if your parenting values are far apart, that difference matters long before a lease ends. Even if kids aren't imminent, clarity is kinder than drift. Ask more than “Do you want kids, yes or no?” That answer alone doesn't tell you much. Try, “How would parenting change us?” or “What kind of parents would we want to be?” That opens up timelines, discipline, religious upbringing, division of labor, and how much family support you'd expect from each side. Good follow-up questions sound like this: - **What did you like and dislike about your childhood home?** - **How were disagreements handled in your family?** - **What does discipline mean to you?** - **How much would faith or culture shape a child's upbringing?** - **If our answers differ, what would make this workable, if anything?** If one partner says “I'm not sure yet,” that can be a valid answer, as long as there's a real plan to revisit it. Some couples set a future date, others discuss the life stage when the question may become clearer. If the disagreement is fundamental, it may be worth talking with a licensed couples therapist before you build a shared life on an unresolved split. ## 10. How do we envision our future together, and what are our non-negotiable values? Moving in together is rarely just about the apartment. It usually signals that both people are imagining some version of the future, even if they haven't said it out loud yet. That's why this question matters: “What does a good life look like to you?” The answer tells you what each person is trying to build. Write your answers separately first. One of you may picture living close to family, while the other dreams of moving abroad. One person may put career first, while the other wants stability and roots. The point isn't to force identical dreams. It's to find out whether your dreams can coexist without one person vanishing inside the other person's plan. A useful way to talk about this is to name your essentials and then talk about the trade-offs. Honesty, financial security, spirituality, travel, family time, ambition, and home stability can all matter in different ways. Ask what can bend and what can't. Then compare. A few practical prompts help: - **Where do we want to be in five years?** - **What should feel true about our home, work, and family life?** - **What do we refuse to sacrifice just to keep the peace?** - **What would an annual check-in sound like if we stayed aligned?** A shared future works better when both people stay curious. If you want a light way to explore values without turning it into a debate, LoveCheck's **Couple Quiz** in Classic mode can help you compare priorities and spot the places where you're already aligned. ## Moving In Together: 10-Point Comparison | Topic | 🔄 Implementation complexity | ⚡ Resource requirements | 📊 Expected outcomes | 💡 Ideal use cases | ⭐ Key advantages | |---|---:|---:|---|---|---| | How do we handle finances and household expenses? | Medium–High, sensitive negotiations, ongoing upkeep | Moderate, time, budgeting tools, possible account changes | Clear cost-sharing, fewer money-driven conflicts | Moving in, unequal incomes, shared lease or big purchases | Prevents misunderstandings; builds financial trust | | What are our expectations around household chores and cleaning? | Low–Medium, set once, requires maintenance | Low, time coordination, apps, occasional paid help | Fair task distribution; less passive-aggression | Busy schedules, differing cleanliness standards | Removes guesswork; balances responsibility | | How do we balance alone time and together time? | Low, boundary-setting and routines | Low, scheduling, small rituals | Better autonomy; reduced suffocation or resentment | Introvert/extrovert mixes, hectic work lives | Preserves identity; improves appreciation of togetherness | | What are our boundaries around family involvement? | Medium, external relationships require enforcement | Low–Moderate, communication, consistent boundary setting | Reduced family-driven drama; unified couple front | Overbearing families, holiday/visit planning | Protects couple primacy; minimizes boundary violations | | How do we handle conflict and disagreements? | Medium–High, habit change and agreed protocols | Moderate, time, practice, possible therapy | Safer fights; faster repair and less festering | Recurring arguments, differing conflict styles | Reduces escalation; ensures both feel heard | | What does intimacy and physical affection look like for each of us? | Medium, vulnerability and ongoing check-ins | Low–Moderate, time, communication, optional counseling | Clearer sexual/affection expectations; less pressure | Libido mismatches, post-move intimacy changes | Increases safety around desire; prevents resentment | | How do we handle stress, work, and mental health? | Medium–High, requires empathy and systems | Moderate–High, check-ins, rituals, professional support | Better mutual support; fewer spillovers into relationship | High-stress jobs, mental-health concerns | Builds empathy; normalizes seeking help | | What are our expectations around social media, privacy, and technology? | Low–Medium, habit and boundary agreements | Low, rules, device habits, tagging consent | Clear public/private lines; improved in-person focus | Public profiles, privacy-sensitive partners | Protects privacy; reduces online misunderstandings | | Do we want kids, and if so, what does parenting look like? | High, long-term values and life plans | Significant, emotional, time, financial planning | Alignment on family goals or early identification of incompatibility | Serious/long-term commitments, pre-family planning | Prevents life-changing surprises; clarifies future choices | | How do we envision our future together, and what are our non-negotiable values? | High, deep reflection and honest negotiation | Moderate, time for visioning, regular check-ins | Shared direction or early recognition of divergence | Pre-marital planning, long-term commitments | Clarifies priorities; guides major life decisions | ## Turn the Answers Into a Shared Home Plan The best moving-in conversations do more than reveal compatibility. They create a home plan you can live with. Write down the agreements that matter, even if they're imperfect at first, because memory gets selective once rent is due, dishes pile up, or one of you has a rough week. A written note in your phone, a shared doc, or a paper page on the fridge can keep both of you honest about what you decided together. Don't try to solve everything in one sitting. Pick a few trial rules and treat them like a first draft. Maybe you test a chore schedule for a month, use a spending check-in every payday, or agree to a phone-free dinner once a week. Then set a monthly or quarterly revisit date so the system can change with your lives. Finances shift. Work stress changes. Sleep needs change. Family boundaries change. Even the best agreement needs a check-in. A simple next step helps keep the conversation moving. Each partner can choose one question that felt easy, one that needs more time, and one action to try this week. Maybe the action is opening a shared spreadsheet, planning a calm talk about family boundaries, or setting a bedtime phone rule. Small follow-through matters more than perfect wording. LoveCheck can support that follow-through without turning it into homework. The **Couple Quiz** helps you compare answers, the **Daily Love Quests** keep connection visible, the **Love Calendar** shows what you've been doing, the **Days Together counter** gives your time together a clear marker, and the **Mood of the Day** prompt makes emotional check-ins easier to start. It's a lightweight way to keep the conversation alive after the move instead of letting everything fade into routine. LoveCheck is relationship wellness support, not therapy or medical care. If you're dealing with abuse, addiction, betrayal, or a mental-health crisis, the right next step is a licensed professional. If the issue is staying connected while building a home together, start with one honest answer tonight and one practical agreement tomorrow. --- LoveCheck makes it easier to turn awkward talks into steady habits. Use the Couple Quiz, Daily Love Quests, and simple check-ins to keep your moving-in conversations active after the lease is signed. If you want a lightweight way to stay aligned as partners, visit [LoveCheck](https://www.lovecheckapp.com).

5. How do we handle conflict and disagreements?

Every couple has conflict. The question is whether your home becomes a place where arguments spiral or a place where both of you know how to reset. Research on relationship outcomes suggests that timing and communication patterns matter, and couples who cohabit before engagement have shown less favorable outcomes than those who live together later in the commitment process (IFStudies executive summary). That doesn't mean conflict is doomed, it means the way you handle it deserves real attention.

Ask this early: “When you're upset, do you want to talk immediately, or do you need time alone first?” One partner may need to cool down in silence. The other may need quick reassurance. Neither style is wrong. The problem starts when each person assumes their own style is the only reasonable one.

A better conflict plan can sound like this:

If we're both calm, we come back to the conversation. If either of us is flooded, we take space and set a time to return.

That one sentence prevents a lot of half-finished fights. You can also agree on a soft restart phrase, like “Can we try that again more gently?” It sounds simple, but it can interrupt a sharp tone before the whole conversation turns defensive.

A few ground rules help:

  • Use “I” statements. “I felt unheard when...” lands better than “You always...”
  • Don't fight when hungry, tired, or overloaded. That's not weakness, it's timing.
  • Write it down if talking gets too hot. Some couples do better exchanging notes and then talking later.
  • End with one concrete next step. “Who's taking the groceries?” is often better than a dramatic emotional truce that solves nothing.

If you want a practice space for kinder conversations, LoveCheck's Daily Love Quests can support lighter vulnerability, and these couple therapy exercises at home can help you build the habit of repairing instead of rehearsing the same argument.

6. What does intimacy and physical affection look like for each of us?

Intimacy gets redefined once you share a home. Sometimes that means more affection because you're around each other more. Sometimes it means less spontaneity because daily logistics start crowding out desire. A useful conversation starts with touch, not just sex, because people often need different kinds of closeness to feel wanted.

Try asking, “What kind of physical affection makes you feel loved?” That can open the door to real answers. One partner might love hand-holding, forehead kisses, or hugging in the kitchen. The other might feel closest through acts of service and only warm up to touch after stress has settled. Neither is a problem. It's just information.

A few ways couples make this more workable:

  • Talk about non-sexual touch first. It's easier and usually less loaded.
  • Schedule intimacy if spontaneity isn't happening. Planned time can be respectful, not mechanical.
  • Create a low-pressure opt-out signal. A simple “not tonight” without shame keeps rejection from turning into a fight.
  • Check in about stress and libido. Desire changes with life, and that's normal.
  • Talk about privacy. Shared housing changes when and how you get personal space.

A direct but gentle question helps: “Are we both happy with our physical connection right now? What would feel better?” If you want a more playful entry point, LoveCheck's Couple Quiz in Spicy mode can help you compare preferences without making the first conversation feel clinical. For a deeper prompt set, questions to feel closer to your partner can help you move past surface-level answers.

7. How do we handle stress, work, and mental health?

Stress does not stay at the office door, and it does not respect relationship timing either. One person may come home full of words and need to vent for 20 minutes. The other may need quiet first. If you don't talk about that difference, stress can get misread as coldness, criticism, or withdrawal.

Ask, “When you're stressed, do you want to talk, be distracted, or be left alone?” That question gives your partner a choice instead of forcing them into your preferred style of support. A person who needs decompression might say, “I'm running on empty. Give me 30 minutes and then I'll be more present.” That's much kinder than disappearing without explanation.

A few supportive habits go a long way:

  • Use a low-energy signal. “I need extra grace today” can prevent unnecessary tension.
  • Create a check-in ritual. A quick “1 to 10, how are you doing?” helps you notice patterns.
  • Keep work stress out of every meal. Phone-free dinner or bedtime protects the relationship from becoming a second workplace.
  • Support professional help when needed. If depression, anxiety, addiction, betrayal, or a mental-health crisis is in the picture, reach out to a licensed professional.

Helpful truth: You're not responsible for solving your partner's stress, but you are responsible for how you show up around it.

LoveCheck's Mood of the Day can make these check-ins feel less forced. It gives you a simple way to notice emotional weather before a bad day turns into a bad week.

8. What are our expectations around social media, privacy, and technology?

A lot of couples say they've talked about “privacy” when they've really only talked about passwords. Those are not the same thing. The core question is how public you want your relationship to be, and how protected each person wants their private life to remain.

Start with something simple: “How do you feel about sharing couple stuff online?” Some people love anniversary posts and vacation photos. Others want their relationship to stay mostly offline. Neither preference is strange. Trouble starts when one person posts freely and the other feels exposed or controlled.

The most useful boundaries are concrete:

  • No posting arguments. Relationship struggles stay private.
  • Ask before tagging. That gives both people agency over their image.
  • Keep phones out of the bedroom. Sleep and intimacy both benefit.
  • Make dinner phone-free at least once a week. Even one protected meal can change the tone of a week.
  • Respect special privacy needs. If someone has trauma from an ex sharing personal details, that matters.

If one partner has a public-facing job, discuss what that means for photos, captions, and location sharing. Fame doesn't have to be the issue, visibility does. The same goes for couples who prefer to keep love offline. You don't need a public explanation for wanting privacy.

LoveCheck's privacy page is a good reminder that privacy is part of trust, not an afterthought. Make the same standard true in your home.

9. Do we want kids, and if so, what does parenting look like?

This is one of those questions to ask before moving in together that can feel too big for a rental conversation, but it isn't. If one person wants children and the other doesn't, or if your parenting values are far apart, that difference matters long before a lease ends. Even if kids aren't imminent, clarity is kinder than drift.

Ask more than “Do you want kids, yes or no?” That answer alone doesn't tell you much. Try, “How would parenting change us?” or “What kind of parents would we want to be?” That opens up timelines, discipline, religious upbringing, division of labor, and how much family support you'd expect from each side.

Good follow-up questions sound like this:

  • What did you like and dislike about your childhood home?
  • How were disagreements handled in your family?
  • What does discipline mean to you?
  • How much would faith or culture shape a child's upbringing?
  • If our answers differ, what would make this workable, if anything?

If one partner says “I'm not sure yet,” that can be a valid answer, as long as there's a real plan to revisit it. Some couples set a future date, others discuss the life stage when the question may become clearer. If the disagreement is fundamental, it may be worth talking with a licensed couples therapist before you build a shared life on an unresolved split.

10. How do we envision our future together, and what are our non-negotiable values?

Moving in together is rarely just about the apartment. It usually signals that both people are imagining some version of the future, even if they haven't said it out loud yet. That's why this question matters: “What does a good life look like to you?” The answer tells you what each person is trying to build.

Write your answers separately first. One of you may picture living close to family, while the other dreams of moving abroad. One person may put career first, while the other wants stability and roots. The point isn't to force identical dreams. It's to find out whether your dreams can coexist without one person vanishing inside the other person's plan.

A useful way to talk about this is to name your essentials and then talk about the trade-offs. Honesty, financial security, spirituality, travel, family time, ambition, and home stability can all matter in different ways. Ask what can bend and what can't. Then compare.

A few practical prompts help:

  • Where do we want to be in five years?
  • What should feel true about our home, work, and family life?
  • What do we refuse to sacrifice just to keep the peace?
  • What would an annual check-in sound like if we stayed aligned?

A shared future works better when both people stay curious. If you want a light way to explore values without turning it into a debate, LoveCheck's Couple Quiz in Classic mode can help you compare priorities and spot the places where you're already aligned.

Turn the Answers Into a Shared Home Plan

The best moving-in conversations do more than reveal compatibility. They create a home plan you can live with. Write down the agreements that matter, even if they're imperfect at first, because memory gets selective once rent is due, dishes pile up, or one of you has a rough week. A written note in your phone, a shared doc, or a paper page on the fridge can keep both of you honest about what you decided together.

Don't try to solve everything in one sitting. Pick a few trial rules and treat them like a first draft. Maybe you test a chore schedule for a month, use a spending check-in every payday, or agree to a phone-free dinner once a week. Then set a monthly or quarterly revisit date so the system can change with your lives. Finances shift. Work stress changes. Sleep needs change. Family boundaries change. Even the best agreement needs a check-in.

A simple next step helps keep the conversation moving. Each partner can choose one question that felt easy, one that needs more time, and one action to try this week. Maybe the action is opening a shared spreadsheet, planning a calm talk about family boundaries, or setting a bedtime phone rule. Small follow-through matters more than perfect wording.
